articles.title: ‘May compromise security’: Delhi HC upholds IAF decision to withhold details of PM Modi, Manmohan Singh’s foreign visits
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court has upheld the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) decision to deny access to records of foreign visits undertaken by Prime Minister
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court has upheld the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) decision to deny access to records of foreign visits undertaken by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his predecessor, Manmohan Singh, setting aside a Central Information Commission (CIC) order directing the force to disclose the flight records.Justice Amit Mahajan ruled that the CIC had "erred" in its July 2020 order directing the IAF to disclose Special Flight Returns (SFR-II), even after redacting the names and identifying details of security personnel.The judge observed that removing such details would not necessarily eliminate potential security risks.Justice Mahajan rejected the petitioner's argument that the information was a matter of significant public interest as it concerned expenditure on foreign visits funded by taxpayers.Counsel for the petitioner, Commodore (retired) Lokesh Batra, argued that the request sought details of private individuals who accompanied the prime ministers at public expense, not the identities of security personnel.“The mere fact that public funds have been expended on the foreign visits of the Hon’ble prime minister does not, by itself, justify disclosure of information which may compromise the security arrangements put in place for such visits,” the judge observed.The high court held that once the competent authority (IAF) concluded that disclosing the information could jeopardise national security or the prime ministers' safety, neither the CIC nor the court could override the assessment of the security agencies responsible for their protection.Citing Supreme Court judgments on exemptions under the RTI Act, the court reiterated that the right to information (RTI) is not absolute and must be balanced against other protected interests, including national security and the confidentiality of sensitive information.Justice Mahajan noted that Section 8(1)(a) of the RTI Act exempts information whose disclosure could adversely affect the security or strategic interests of the State, while Section 8(1)(g) protects information whose disclosure could endanger a person’s life or physical safety.Holding that the IAF was justified in invoking these exemptions, the high court allowed the petition and set aside the CIC’s order. It also disposed of all pending applications.The caseThe case arose from an RTI application Batra filed on June 5, 2018, seeking details of prime ministers’ foreign visits on IAF aircraft from April 1, 2013, until the date of his application.The IAF provided some information about PM Modi’s foreign travel but stated that Manmohan Singh had not travelled on IAF aircraft between April 1, 2013, and May 25, 2014.However, it refused to provide copies of the Special Flight Returns (SFR), Parts I and II, citing national security concerns and the confidential nature of the records.The IAF maintained that the documents contained sensitive details about the aircraft, aircrew, passengers and Special Protection Group (SPG) personnel accompanying the prime minister. It argued that disclosure, particularly when combined with information already available in the public domain, could reveal details of the prime minister’s security arrangements.After the First Appellate Authority rejected Batra’s appeal in September 2018, he approached the CIC. The commission directed the IAF to provide certified copies of the available and relevant SFR-II records, prompting the force to challenge the order before the high court.During the proceedings, the IAF argued that the records contained interconnected details, including passengers’ designations, appointments, identification numbers, flight references, passenger numbers and agency particulars. It stated that disclosing these details could help identify security personnel, reveal the composition of the prime ministers' entourage and allow inferences about security deployment patterns.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Man sells everything and travels 1,200 miles to meet his online girlfriend. It doesn’t end well when he learns the truth about her
articles.summary: Selling everything for love is a big gamble. But one Brazilian man took that risk, traveling more than 1,200 miles to meet a woman he hoped to marry. Unfortu...
articles.body:
Selling everything for love is a big gamble. But one Brazilian man took that risk, traveling more than 1,200 miles to meet a woman he hoped to marry. Unfortunately, the woman he had fallen for wasn't even real.

Online romance has led people to lose thousands to fake lovers or expect marriage before even meeting someone . But this man's search for love ended with a strange discovery, and he had already sacrificed almost everything for it.

According to the New York Post , 49-year-old Brazilian bricklayer Edimar Martins sold his belongings to travel from Maranhão to Belo Horizonte, hoping to meet a woman named Jessica Oliveira. Instead, he discovered that his dream partner was an AI-generated character.

Martins first came across Jessica's social media profile in 2020. He believed she was real and eventually decided she could be his future wife. On October 9, he sold his possessions to afford a bus ticket to Belo Horizonte, more than 1,200 miles from his home.

"I sold all my things, I got rid of everything," Martins told TV Mirante . He arrived on October 11, expecting to finally meet Jessica. But after failing to find her, he approached a local radio station for assistance.

"I went to the radio station there, and they said no, that's fake news, that woman doesn't exist," he recalled. The woman he had traveled across Brazil to meet was actually an AI-generated character.

Jessica appeared on a TikTok account called @jessicafazendeira, which reportedly had around 300,000 followers. The videos portrayed her as a woman living on a farm who was looking for a romantic partner.

In one video that has since been deleted, the character promised financial support to whoever agreed to live with her. "I really want to support you, I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life," the AI-generated woman declared.

After Martins' experience attracted attention, the person operating the TikTok account addressed the controversy. In a video posted Wednesday, the account owner acknowledged that Jessica was created using AI but denied ever communicating directly with Martins.

"I came here to state the obvious: I am made of artificial intelligence," the statement began. The account was reportedly created to generate online engagement for commercial purposes rather than arrange relationships.

"I never spoke directly to anyone, much less took anyone to Belo Horizonte. It was a surprise to me to see what is happening," the account owner explained.

Meanwhile, Martins was stranded in Belo Horizonte after spending his money on the journey. He eventually approached City Hall for assistance when he could no longer afford to return home.

During a conversation with a social worker, Martins explained that he had traveled such a long distance because he was tired of being alone. He wanted to find someone to share his life with.

"It only brings sadness, discouragement, depression. Many people wanted to find a relationship, so I came," he admitted. He subsequently received assistance to return home.

Despite the disappointment, Martins hasn't abandoned his hopes of finding a partner. He is reportedly staying with a family member and has expressed an interest in returning to Belo Horizonte.

Surprisingly, he wants to find love in the same city where his expectations fell apart. "I didn't find her, but I'll find another one, and it will be in the same place I went, and I'll go again," he declared.

Martins' experience shows how convincing AI-generated personalities can appear online. The TikTok account attracted hundreds of thousands of followers, but he took his belief in the fictional character much further.

He lost his belongings and traveled across Brazil for someone who never existed. Yet, despite everything, he still believes he can find a real partner.

articles.title: Colombia illegal gold mine collapse kills 14 people
articles.summary: Illegal gold mine collapse in southwestern Colombia leaves 14 people dead, 7 injured.
articles.body:
The collapse of an illegal gold mine in southwestern Colombia killed 14 people and injured seven others, local authorities said on Monday.

The accident took place in the rural Chambero sector of the Santa Barbara de Iscuande municipality, located in the department of Narino.

Search and rescue operations have concluded, Narino Governor Luis Alfonso Escobar said.

Jorge Tovar Castillo, a disaster response official in Narino, said that an additional 12 to 15 miners have been reported as missing following the accident.

He said that municipal authorities were handling the response but added that communication had been difficult.

Santa Barbara de Iscuande is surrounded by dense rainforest and can only be reached by boat or small aircraft.

In a message on X, Escobar said the gold mine was an “informal” mine.

Informal and unregulated mining is common in rural parts of Colombia, where operations often lack adequate safety infrastructure, leading to frequent fatal accidents.

“At this moment our priority is to save lives, accompany families and guarantee an opportune response to this painful tragedy,” Escobar wrote.

In August, 13 people died in a similar mining accident in the municipality of Policarpa, also in Narino.

articles.title: Mahmoud Khalil takes deportation fight to the US Supreme Court
articles.summary: Lawyers for the former student leader seek to overturn an appeals court decision that would allow for his removal.
articles.body:
Pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil has petitioned the United States Supreme Court to review a court ruling that could pave the way for his re-arrest and deportation.

On Monday, Khalil’s lawyers filed an emergency application to the high court, seeking an immediate stay of a decision from Philadelphia’s 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.

That court had ruled that federal law should have prohibited lower courts from ordering Khalil’s release from immigration detention in June 2025.

Instead, the appeals court said that Khalil’s detention should have been weighed first in an immigration court — a system overseen by the executive branch of the US government — and not in district court, which is part of the judicial branch.

In March 2025, Khalil became the first student protester known to be targeted for his pro-Palestinian views under the second administration of President Donald Trump.

A permanent US resident and former Columbia University graduate student, Khalil was arrested inside the student housing complex where he lived with his wife, a US citizen.

The push to deport Khalil has become a flashpoint in the debate over free speech on US campuses.

His petition to the Supreme Court could result in a major legal showdown that determines whether federal courts can intervene when noncitizens face retaliatory detention for speech protected under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

Khalil’s lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to rule that noncitizens do indeed have the right to sue if immigration officials detain them as a reprisal for exercising free speech.

“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech,” Khalil said during a news conference on Monday.

Trump campaigned for re-election in 2024 in part on a pledge to crack down on the pro-Palestinian student protest movement, which had erupted in 2023.

Columbia University in New York became an epicentre for such activism. Khalil, who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, had served as a spokesperson for the protest groups.

The Trump administration, however, has characterised pro-Palestinian activism as a threat to US foreign policy interests. It has argued it has the legal right to deport noncitizens who engage in such protests as a result.

After his arrest, Khalil was quickly moved to immigration detention centres in New Jersey, then Louisiana, where he remained in custody for more than three months.

Khalil faces deportation to Algeria or Syria if the 3rd Circuit Court’s decision holds.

In May, the 3rd Circuit narrowly voted six-to-five against reconsidering his case, but its decision will not go into effect until Khalil has exhausted his appeals.

He has fought his deportation both in the immigration court system and in the federal district court system, where he has filed a habeas corpus case. Both cases remain ongoing.

In April, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied his appeal in the immigration court system and issued a final order of removal in his case.

On Monday, faculty and staff at Columbia University held a silent vigil outside one of the school’s gates to protest what they described as “abducted students”, taken by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Placards with portraits of Khalil and fellow student protester Mohsen Mahdawi, among others, were hoisted into the air. Demonstrators called for solidarity with the students facing deportation and pushed for Columbia University to reopen its gates to the public after their closure during the protest movement.

articles.title: Guardar dinheiro é investir? Veja o que muda entre as duas opções | G1
articles.standfirst: Entenda como o destino do dinheiro pode fazer diferença ao longo do tempo.
articles.summary: Entenda como o destino do dinheiro pode fazer diferença ao longo do tempo.
articles.body:
Para muitas pessoas, guardar dinheiro é como colocar uma meta no bolso. Porém, embora separado e disponível, o destino dado ao recurso é o que pode, de fato, fazer a diferença ao longo do tempo. A partir disso, poupar e investir tomam rumos diferentes, principalmente, quando entram em jogo fatores como rentabilidade, liquidez e o objetivo para o qual o valor foi separado.

Gerente da Agência Sicoob, em Cabo Frio, na Região dos Lagos, Rebeca Cristina Valdo Thomaz explica que, deixar o dinheiro parado, sem qualquer aplicação ou rendimento, faz com que o saldo permaneça o mesmo. Porém, considerando a diminuição da capacidade de compra com o passar dos meses, é aconselhável que esta decisão seja reavaliada.

“Os preços variam por conta da inflação, enquanto o dinheiro permanece no mesmo lugar. Sendo assim, os R$ 500 de hoje não necessariamente terão o mesmo poder de compra daqui a algum tempo. É uma perda que nem sempre é percebida na conta, mas sentida diretamente durante uma ida ao mercado ou pagamento de alguma despesa”, exemplificou.

Gerente da Agência Sicoob, em Cabo Frio, na Região dos Lagos, Rebeca Cristina Valdo Thomaz — Foto: Divulgação

O dinheiro na conta corrente normalmente é mantido pela praticidade e disponibilidade para as movimentações do dia a dia, enquanto a poupança é considerada um investimento simples, com regras próprias de remuneração e liquidez. Para Rebeca, há também alternativas no mercado, cada uma com características próprias de rentabilidade, prazo, liquidez e risco.

“Entender o destino que será dado ao dinheiro é fundamental para definir a opção mais adequada, transformando o esforço de economizar em um plano concreto, sendo possível estabelecer objetivos e acompanhar o progresso. Não existe uma única opção de investimento que seja a mais adequada para todas as pessoas e situações”, afirma.

No Sicoob, a educação financeira estimula o associado a compreender seus próprios objetivos, avaliando assim, alternativas de investimentos e condições que podem variar de acordo com o produto, o valor e o período da aplicação. Entre as principais modalidades disponíveis, estão Renda Fixa, Fundos de Investimentos e Renda Variável.

“O mais importante é que o cooperado tenha a orientação necessária para tomar uma decisão consciente e não simplesmente escolher uma aplicação sem entender como ela funciona. Entendemos que não é preciso ter muito dinheiro para começar e nem é preciso esperar juntar uma grande quantia. Respeitar a própria realidade financeira e criar o hábito de investir regularmente é o que importa”, destacou a gerente do Sicoob.

Ainda segundo Rebeca, investir não significa necessariamente deixar o dinheiro preso. A organização financeira pode combinar valores disponíveis para emergências, com aplicações voltadas a objetivos de médio e longo prazo. “Se poupar é o primeiro passo, planejar como e quando utilizar o que foi acumulado também faz parte da decisão”, concluiu.

Agência Sicoob, em Cabo Frio, na Região dos Lagos — Foto: Divulgação

Instituição financeira cooperativa, o Sicoob reúne mais de 10,2 milhões de cooperados e está presente em todos os estados brasileiros e no Distrito Federal. Oferece um portfólio completo de soluções financeiras, incluindo conta corrente, crédito, investimentos, cartões, previdência, consórcios, seguros, cobrança bancária e meios eletrônicos de pagamento. articles.title: Zelensky diz que sistema da SpaceX usado na guerra ficou mais lento e afeta tropas ucranianas | G1
articles.standfirst: Zelensky também acusou os Estados Unidos de atrasar a entrega de mísseis interceptadores de que seu país precisa para se proteger dos ataques russos.
articles.summary: Zelensky também acusou os Estados Unidos de atrasar a entrega de mísseis interceptadores de que seu país precisa para se proteger dos ataques russos.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky acusa Donald Trump de querer forçar a Ucrânia a se render — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

As tropas ucranianas estão sendo prejudicadas por uma redução na velocidade dos sistemas de satélites americanos, usadas no campo de batalha para coordenar ataques de drones contra as forças armadas russas, informou o presidente ucraniano, Volodimir Zelensky, nesta segunda-feira (19).

Zelensky afirmou que as unidades na linha de frente afirmaram que os equipamentos do “pararam de operar a 130-160 milhas por hora em vários setores do front”.

Na semana passada, a Ucrânia acusou os Estados Unidos de reduzirem literalmente a velocidade desse sistema de satélites, pertencente à empresa SpaceX, de Elon Musk, após o presidente Donald Trump criticar os ataques ucranianos contra refinarias russas.

A Ucrânia utiliza o Starshield para comunicações no campo de batalha, para ataques de médio alcance em território ocupado pela Rússia e para seus drones interceptadores; o país também emprega o Starlink para fins civis.

As autoridades ucranianas afirmaram, na semana passada, que não conseguiram alertar a população civil sobre ataques iminentes com mísseis e drones até depois do impacto desses projetos.

Zelensky também acusou, nesta segunda-feira, os Estados Unidos de atrasar a entrega de mísseis interceptadores de que seu país precisa para se proteger dos ataques russos.

Ele garantiu aos senadores americanos que “o Pentágono está atrasando a entrega de mísseis já pagos” por países europeus para a Ucrânia. Afirmou que o lote “está aguardando a assinatura de [Pete] Hegseth”, o secretário de Defesa dos Estados Unidos.

Suas queixas coincidem com os esforços renovados entre o líder ucraniano e Trump, que nesta segunda afirmou que aceitaria uma proposta do presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, de se reunir com ele e com o líder chinês, Xi Jinping , para discutir a guerra na Ucrânia.

A reunião pode ocorrer durante a cúpula do fórum de Cooperação Econômica Ásia-Pacífico (Apec), nos dias 18 e 19 de novembro, na cidade chinesa de Shenzhen.

articles.title: 'Mata logo': vítimas relatam supostas torturas em torcida organizada  | G1
articles.standfirst: Investigação do MP aponta que presidente e diretores usavam martelos, facas e tacos contra membros sob pretexto de apurar desvios internos.
articles.summary: Investigação do MP aponta que presidente e diretores usavam martelos, facas e tacos contra membros sob pretexto de apurar desvios internos.
articles.body:
Uma sala localizada no subsolo da sede da Bamor, principal torcida organizada do Esporte Clube Bahia, é apontada pelas autoridades como palco de sessões de tortura promovidas por integrantes da direção da entidade. A investigação, conduzida pelo Ministério Público da Bahia, reúne relatos de vítimas, áudios e apreensões feitas durante uma operação policial realizada no fim de setembro.

O caso ganhou impulso após o acesso dos investigadores a mensagens de áudio atribuídas ao presidente da torcida, Matheus Pires Castro, nas quais são descritas agressões contra pessoas consideradas suspeitas de irregularidades internas. Em um dos trechos, ele afirma: "Amanhã a gente vai pegar ele daquele jeito. Vai ser uma cena triste". Em outro, diz que o alvo deveria sair "com a mão esmagada".

Uma das vítimas, que integrou a organizada por 18 anos e chegou a ocupar funções de liderança, afirma ter sido convocada para prestar esclarecimentos sobre uma suposta fraude envolvendo o cadastro de sócios.

Segundo seu relato, a reunião rapidamente se transformou em uma sequência de agressões.

"Começaram a me bater com o martelo. Depois pegaram minha mão, atravessaram minha mão de faca, me deram quatro facadas na mão. Pegaram um taco de beisebol de madeira e começaram a desferir golpes. Botaram um saco na minha cabeça para me sufocar", afirmou.

A vítima diz que, apesar das acusações, os dirigentes não conseguiram comprovar sua participação em qualquer desvio de recursos.

"Eu fui agredido inicialmente pelo presidente e, após isso, o quadro de diretores iniciou um processo de quatro horas de tortura comigo. Também houve agressões psicológicas, dizendo que eu deveria assumir e que iam atrás da minha família."

Outro homem ouvido pela reportagem prestava serviços de tecnologia para a organizada. Assim como a primeira vítima, ele afirma ter sido acusado de envolvimento em desvios financeiros.

Segundo o relato, a agressão começou depois que ele sugeriu levar o caso à polícia.

"Me chamaram para uma sala. Eu não imaginaria que seria uma sala de tortura. Quando falei que a gente deveria ir para a delegacia prestar queixa, comecei a ser agredido com esse taco de beisebol nas pernas, nos braços e nas costas. Depois vieram muitos chutes e pontapés."

Ele afirma que a violência ocorreu diante de integrantes da diretoria da torcida.

"Nessa sala estavam o presidente e o vice-presidente. Também ouvi eles mandando: 'Mata logo'."

O homem ainda relata que, durante as cerca de quatro horas de agressões, foi obrigado a fornecer a senha do celular e teve mais de R$ 5 mil retirados de sua conta bancária. No dia seguinte, procurou a polícia para denunciar o caso.

No fim de setembro, uma operação conjunta do Ministério Público da Bahia e das polícias Civil e Militar cumpriu mandados de prisão e de busca contra integrantes da Bamor. Entre os presos estavam o presidente, Matheus Pires Castro, e o vice-presidente, Luciano Venâncio.

Durante as buscas, os agentes apreenderam um taco de beisebol, martelos e um alicate. As vítimas afirmaram reconhecer os objetos como os mesmos utilizados nas agressões relatadas

De acordo com o Ministério Público, as pessoas eram atraídas para reuniões na sede da torcida e submetidas a intenso sofrimento físico e psicológico com o objetivo de obter confissões.

Em nota, as defesas de Matheus Pires Castro e Luciano Venâncio afirmaram que os dois são inocentes e que todas as medidas judiciais cabíveis estão sendo adotadas.

O caso ocorre em um contexto de preocupação das autoridades com episódios de violência envolvendo torcidas organizadas na Bahia. Desde 2017, clássicos entre Bahia e Vitória são disputados com torcida única dentro dos estádios, medida adotada para tentar reduzir confrontos entre grupos rivais. Ainda assim, ocorrências violentas continuam sendo registradas fora dos locais das partidas.

Para o Ministério Público, os crimes investigados não podem ser confundidos com a atuação da maioria dos torcedores.

"Deveria ser uma entidade voltada a valorizar o esporte e a confraternização. O que se pratica no seu seio são atos de violência dessa natureza", afirmou o promotor responsável pelo caso.

articles.title: Adoção de irmãos em Goiás: casal italiano conta como formou família | G1
articles.standfirst: Nicola D'Alba e Maria Cristofaro se conheceram aos 44 anos e já compartilhavam o desejo de adotar. Durante uma viagem a Lourdes, na França, o casal decidiu seguir esse caminho e, anos depois, adotou dois irmãos brasileiros.
articles.summary: Após decidirem pela adoção de irmãos em Goiás durante viagem à França, o casal italiano Nicola D'Alba e Maria Cristofaro compartilha a emoção de formar uma família internacional.
articles.body:
Uma viagem a Lourdes, na França, ajudou o casal italiano Nicola D'Alba e Maria Cristofaro a tomar uma decisão que mudaria a vida deles e de dois irmãos brasileiros, de 8 e 9 anos. Os dois já conversavam sobre adoção desde que se conheceram, aos 44 anos, mas foi durante a viagem que, segundo Nicola, acontecimentos os fizeram perceber que aquele poderia ser o caminho para formar uma família.

Anos depois, o casal adotou os irmãos que viviam em uma instituição de acolhimento em São Luís de Montes Belos , no oeste de Goiás. A história foi compartilhada em vídeos divulgados pelo Tribunal de Justiça de Goiás (TJ-GO), nos quais Nicola e Maria relembram a decisão de adotar e as dificuldades enfrentadas até a chegada das crianças à Itália.

"Tomamos essa decisão porque nos conhecemos quando tínhamos 44 anos. Em nossas experiências, começamos logo a falar sobre adoção", contou Nicola, em depoimento traduzido do italiano.

Antes de conhecer Maria, Nicola trabalhou em um centro de acolhimento para imigrantes. Já ela participou de atividades ligadas à Igreja Católica e realizou viagens à África. Segundo o italiano, essas experiências contribuíram para que os dois conversassem sobre adoção desde o início do relacionamento.

A viagem a Lourdes, cidade francesa conhecida pelo turismo religioso, foi um momento importante nessa decisão. Nicola não detalhou quais acontecimentos marcaram a visita, mas contou que eles ajudaram o casal a reconhecer o caminho que desejava seguir.

"Depois, foi uma viagem a Lourdes em que aconteceram eventos que nos fizeram entender que talvez esse fosse o nosso caminho. E tomamos essa decisão, olhamos nos olhos um do outro, queríamos construir algo bonito", relatou.

A decisão deu início a um processo que, anos depois, aproximaria o casal de duas crianças que viviam a milhares de quilômetros de distância, em Goiás.

Casal italiano Nicola D'Alba e Maria Cristofaro com os dois irmãos adotados em Goiás, antes da mudança da família para a Itália — Foto: Divulgação/TJ GO

A aproximação entre os italianos e as crianças começou por meio de seis videochamadas autorizadas pela Justiça. Para tentar diminuir a distância e superar a dificuldade de comunicação, Nicola e Maria chegaram a preparar um teatro de bonecos durante um dos encontros virtuais.

Depois dessa etapa, viajaram ao Brasil e foram a São Luís de Montes Belos, onde uma audiência marcou o início do estágio de convivência. Os irmãos deixaram a instituição de acolhimento e seguiram com o casal para Goiânia .

Foram 30 dias juntos, período em que precisaram se adaptar à convivência, às diferenças culturais e à barreira do idioma. A família recebeu 15 visitas da equipe técnica, que elaborou relatórios para auxiliar a decisão judicial.

Em outro trecho do depoimento, Nicola reconheceu que o processo exigiu esforço dos quatro.

"Não foi nada simples. Mas sempre olhamos nos olhos um do outro. Apesar dos problemas, apesar de tantas vezes não saber o que fazer [...], o nosso desejo era criar uma linda família, e conseguimos", afirmou, em tradução do italiano.

A adoção foi autorizada em 27 de agosto pelo juiz Ageu de Alencar Miranda, da Vara da Infância e Juventude de São Luís de Montes Belos. Na sentença, o magistrado escreveu uma mensagem em italiano para desejar boas-vindas à família.

Com a decisão, os irmãos viajaram para Bari, no sul da Itália, onde passaram a morar com Nicola e Maria. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo TJ-GO, as crianças foram apresentadas aos avós, tios e outros parentes e começaram a frequentar a escola.

O acompanhamento da família continuará por dois anos, conforme as regras do processo de adoção internacional.

articles.summary: No Paraná, agronegócio, indústrias, logística, transformação digital, saúde, energia e infraestrutura são os setores que devem estar mais aquecidos.
articles.body:
Guia Salarial faz previsões sobre o mercado de trabalho no Paraná. — Foto: Foto: Agência Brasil

Um levantamento feito pela consultoria Robert Half aponta que as áreas de Finanças, Logística, Tecnologia da Informação, Comercial, Desenvolvimento de Negócios, Recursos Humanos e Compras devem liderar as contratações no Paraná em 2027.

A pesquisa mostra ainda quais cargos estarão em alta e uma previsão dos salários das vagas. O levantamento considera o cenário de remunerações da capital paranaense . Veja detalhes abaixo.

Conforme o levantamento, o agronegócio e as indústrias multinacionais e de manufatura serão os segmentos mais aquecidos no estado no próximo ano.

Além disso, também há destaque para empresas de logística e transporte, tecnologia aplicada aos negócios e transformação digital, saúde e farmacêutica, e energia e infraestrutura.

Profissionais mais requisitados no Paraná em 2027

Os profissionais mais demandados em 2027 no Paraná devem ser especialistas fiscais e tributários, para auxiliar as empresas devido à Reforma Tributária. A consultoria ainda aponta que o mercado se queixa da escassez de profissionais seniores nestas áreas, o que pode levar à flexibilização de requisitos técnicos.

Veja lista dos cargos que devem ter mais procura para contratações permanentes:

Especialista/Coordenador/Gerente Tributário

Para contratações por projetos ou temporárias, devem se destacar profissionais que atuam com o planejamento de recursos empresariais e transformação digital, incluindo consultores.

Veja lista dos cargos que devem ter mais procura para contratações por projeto:

Consultores de Implantação ERP (D365, SAP e similares)

Analistas de FP&A para estruturação de indicadores

Especialistas em automação e IA aplicada aos negócios

De acordo com a pesquisa, as empresas paranaenses estão interessadas em reter talentos e em sucessão em posições de liderança. Cresce também a busca pela aplicação da Inteligência Artificial e aumento da produtividade.

"No Paraná, o agronegócio e a indústria seguem como importantes motores do mercado de trabalho, enquanto a Reforma Tributária amplia a demanda por especialistas fiscais e tributários. Ao mesmo tempo, projetos de ERP e transformação digital movimentam contratações temporárias e especializadas", comenta Lesleane Rezende, gerente regional de vendas da Robert Half.

Dos cargos apurados pela pesquisa, o maior salário é o da vaga de Diretor Financeiro (G), na área de liderança executiva. A previsão é de que o cargo tenha uma faixa salarial de R$ 44.750,00 até R$ 71.250,00 . Para empresas de porte P ou M, a média é de R$34.300,00 até R$ 48.000,00

Outro destaque é na área de Engenharia, para o cargo de Diretor de Engenharia (G) de empresas da indústria, com vencimentos de R$ 35.400,00 a R$ 57.000,00. Ainda na mesma área, o Diretor (G) de Cadeia de Suprimentos tem média salarial de R$ 30.900,00 até R$ 49.900,00.

No setor de Marketing, o Gerente Geral (G) pode receber salários de R$ 31.650,00 até R$ 56.100,00.

Outros cargos bem pagos são na área de Tecnologia. A previsão é de que o cargo de Chief Information Officer possa chegar até R$ 47.200,00; o de Chief Security Officer pode chegar a R$ 45.700,00; e o de Chief Technology Officer a R$ 45.040,00.

Os dados consideram apenas a remuneração base, sem incluir bônus ou benefícios, e refletem valores pagos a profissionais conectados pela Robert Half a empregadores no Brasil.

De acordo com a consultoria Robert Half, os salários listados no Guia Salarial resultam de um rigoroso processo multietapas para que as projeções reflitam com precisão o mercado. Eles são baseados na remuneração real de profissionais que a Robert Half conectou a empregadores no Brasil.

As letras “P”, “M” ou “G” (pequeno, médio ou grande), que acompanham alguns cargos, representam o faturamento das empresas. Uma empresa grande é aquela com faturamento acima de R$ 500 milhões. As três faixas de remuneração são definidas pela qualificação e experiência do candidato, além da demanda de mercado para o perfil:

articles.title: Quem era Roberta Felsky Pinheiro, rainha da Oktoberfest morta em SC | G1
articles.standfirst: Turismóloga enfrentava um câncer na língua e morreu no último sábado (17). Organização da maior festa alemã das Américas lamentou perda.
articles.summary: Turismóloga enfrentava um câncer na língua e morreu no último sábado (17). Organização da maior festa alemã das Américas lamentou perda.
articles.body:
Morre ex-rainha da Oktoberfest, Roberta Pinheiro, aos 45 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A turismóloga e comerciante Roberta Felsky Pinheiro , de 45 anos, morreu no último sábado (17) em decorrência de um câncer de língua. Ex-rainha da Oktoberfest de Blumenau (SC) e mãe de três filhos (de 16, 8 e 6 anos), ela foi descrita pelo marido, Jeferson Pinheiro, como uma mulher "forte e iluminada" . Eles eram casados há 16 anos.

Além da formação em turismo, Roberta administrou por alguns anos a loja de calçados da família no Vale do Itajaí. O último trabalho dela foi como servidora na Secretaria Municipal de Planejamento Urbano (Seplan) de Blumenau, em 2024.

" Sempre foi uma mulher ativa e iluminada . A Oktoberfest sempre fez parte da vida dela. Desde pequena, os pais dela tiveram barraca de comida lá na década de 90. Ela era pequena, mas lembrava sempre com muito carinho", contou Jeferson.

Jeferson lembrou ainda que o casal desfilava em um dos grupos tradicionais na festa e, por consequência, Roberta teve vontade de participar do concurso da realeza em 2007, sendo coroada rainha da festa na 24ª edição.

"Ela ganhou como rainha. Sempre falou muito bem e era linda" , relembrou Jeferson, que acompanhou de perto a coroação. Os dois completariam 22 anos de relacionamento em março de 2027.

Oktoberfest manifesta solidariedade à família de ex-rainha morta em SC — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Nas redes sociais, amigos, familiares e grupos ligados à Oktoberfest lamentaram a morte de Roberta. Entre as homenagens está a do Kochkäsewagen, grupo tradicional que desfila no evento.

"Nossa eterna Rainha. Minha sobrinha amada, afilhada e comadre. Seguiu seu caminho, mas ficará para sempre em nossos corações", escreveu uma familiar na publicação da Oktoberfest que anunciou a morte de Roberta.

O velório de Roberta foi realizado no domingo (18) em Blumenau.

Rainha da Oktoberfest — Foto: Oktoberfest/Arquivo

➡️ Composta pela rainha, 1ª princesa e 2ª princesa, a realeza da Oktoberfest atua como embaixadora oficial da festa. Entre as principais funções do trio estão a divulgação e a promoção do evento.

A organização da Oktoberfest Blumenau lamenta profundamente o falecimento de Roberta Felsky Pinheiro, que foi rainha da 24ª edição da festa, realizada em 2007.

Roberta faleceu neste sábado, dia 17 de outubro, após enfrentar um câncer. A organização manifesta sua solidariedade aos familiares e amigos neste momento de dor, desejando força e conforto a todos .

articles.title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced Israel visit
articles.summary: Hegseth has travelled to Israel to meet Netanyahu ahead of a closely contested election, Axios reported, citing sources.
articles.body:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.

The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.

The Reuters news agency could not immediately confirm the visit. The Pentagon and Israel’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and there was no immediate indication of what they discussed.

President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Sunday to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza began.

Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.

“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.

Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.

US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.

“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.

“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

articles.summary: An Australian lawmaker was allegedly hit twice by a driver who made a U-turn before returning to ram into her outside her electoral office, Home Affairs
articles.body: An Australian lawmaker was allegedly hit twice by a driver who made a U-turn before returning to ram into her outside her electoral office, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said, as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the incident as a deliberate act.Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent MP representing Indi, remained in critical condition on Tuesday after undergoing surgery for injuries sustained in the incident in Wangaratta, Victoria, on Monday afternoon. She was initially taken to a local hospital before being airlifted to Melbourne for further treatment."What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time," Burke told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).Albanese said witnesses reported that the driver passed Haines as she stood near the boot of her parked car before turning around and returning to strike her."This wasn't something with a car just going off the road," Albanese told Australian channel News24. "This is something that is very clear was aimed at causing harm to Helen Haines."The motive behind the attack remains unclear, with Albanese urging people not to speculate while investigations continue. Australia's national counterterrorism team, comprising police and intelligence agencies, is investigating the incident.The 43-year-old suspect was arrested at the scene and remained in police custody on Tuesday. No charges had been announced. A knife was also recovered from the suspect, police said.A bystander, identified as barber Ricky Jefferies, rushed out of his shop, pulled the driver from the vehicle and restrained him until police arrived."I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place," Burke said.The incident has renewed concerns over the safety of Australian politicians amid rising hostility towards public officials. Albanese said political discourse had become increasingly polarised, with too much shouting and too little constructive conversation. articles.title: Nearly $1M in sports, Pokémon cards stolen from FedEx truck in California
articles.summary: Thieves made off with nearly $1 million in sports, Pokémon and other trading cards swiped from a FedEx truck in Southern California last week, police said Monday.
articles.body: Thieves made off with nearly $1 million in sports, Pokémon and other trading cards swiped from a FedEx truck in Southern California last week, police said Monday. Officers responded to a trading card authentication company Tuesday about the theft of an estimated $963,000 worth of cards from a FedEx truck, Santa Ana police spokesperson Natalie Garcia said by email. The theft included two pallets of cards and a third that was “disrupted,” she said. The location of the report was Professional Sports Authenticator in the city of Santa Ana, about 33 miles southeast of Los Angeles. The company bills itself on its website as “the leading third-party authentication and grading service” and says it can sell customers’ cards online for a percentage of the selling price to “turn cards into currency.” Nick Andrews, known on social media as the Boston Card Hunter, said on X that there are multiple victims of the theft, one of whom he said lost $500,000 worth of cards. When all is said and done, he said, the heist could be one of the biggest in trading card history. He has compiled a list of cards claimed to have been taken in the theft that numbered as high as 383 on Monday evening. Among them, as the video game news site IGN noted, were a 1995 Upper Deck 23K Gold Michael Jordan card and a 2024 One Piece Simplified Chinese 1st Anniversary Set Nami. Card trader Sky-B, who said he wants to be referred to only under that moniker, discussed cards he said he lost in the theft in a video on YouTube on Monday. “These were 104 cards that I’ve accumulated over two years,” he said. “There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again. And, honestly, that’s what hurts the most — outside of obviously being absolutely financially destroyed here.” He said the missing cards were dropped off at Professional Sports Authenticator, where they were certified and started their journey back to him in Michigan before he discovered they had been stolen. Sky-B said he paid $8,000 in grading fees and lamented that he would be out the likely increased value that the grading added to his cards, which he said were insured up to $156,000 — below their likely market value. A company spokesperson said in an email that grading fees would be returned, along with the fair market value of the cards involved. In a statement, the company said it is working with investigators and has deactivated the stolen cards’ certificates. “We have deactivated the certificates for the stolen items and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items,” a Professional Sports Authenticator spokesperson said. FedEx said in a statement that getting to the bottom of the theft is paramount. “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation,” it said. Garcia, the police spokesperson, said the value of the stolen goods could rise. “It remains an open case,” she said, “and we have not made any arrests or recovered any stolen goods.” In 2024, a FedEx shipment of 54 vintage baseball cards worth $2.1 million was successfully delivered to a Best Western in Strongsville, Ohio, for a sports card conference, but it was stolen by a hotel employee who was sentenced to four to six years in prison, prosecutors in nearby Cleveland said.

articles.title: Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
articles.summary: For many young Tunisians, the question is no longer simply how to make a living, but where they can build a future.
articles.body:
Tunis, Tunisia – For Maher Qassem, the phrase “beyond money” sums up why he is considering leaving his country.

After years of working in the media and trying to secure a stable life for his family, he is now thinking of starting over abroad. Buying a home and planning for a better future have given way to more immediate concerns: covering monthly expenses and meeting mounting financial commitments.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Qassem says almost his entire salary goes towards loan repayments, rent and his son’s education. At times, he adds, he has been unable to help his sick mother pay for medication and treatment.

Qassem is among many young Tunisians who see little meaningful change in their daily lives. Seven years into President Kais Saied’s rule, he worries about his son’s prospects and the quality of life the country can offer future generations.

Others, however, continue to trust the president.

Tunisians remain divided between those who believe the past several years have failed to deliver the change they hoped for and those who still believe reform is possible. These contrasting views unfold against a backdrop of persistent economic difficulties.

Ghaith remembers the excitement surrounding the 2019 presidential election and the expectations raised by Saied’s victory. He was 19 at the time, had little interest in politics, and did not vote. But he recalls the hope that accompanied the president’s election.

Seven years later, Ghaith says, little has changed in his own life.

The cost-of-living pressures that existed then remain, he tells Al Jazeera, while ordinary citizens continue to face recurring difficulties obtaining some essential goods and services.

He is also frustrated by the authorities’ communication with the public. Tunisians want clearer answers about government policies and the results they are expected to deliver, he says. They also want accountability and a clear vision for the future.

For Qassem, the reasons for leaving extend beyond economic hardship. He believes working as a journalist has become more difficult, too.

Not everyone has lost faith in the president.

Mohamed Amine, a taxi driver in his 30s, voted for Saied in the most recent presidential election and remains convinced that he can improve the country’s situation.

The president is “sincere in his intentions” and wants change, Amine tells Al Jazeera. He believes, however, that various obstacles have hindered Saied’s reform programme.

It is too early to judge the outcome, he says. The president should be given more time.

Unemployment, particularly among young people and university graduates, remains a major challenge in Tunisia.

According to the National Institute of Statistics, the unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 622,000 people out of work.

The situation is more severe among younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4 percent, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6 percent. Among female university graduates, it was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent among men.

The desire to leave is widespread. A study by Afrobarometer, an independent African research network that conducts public-opinion surveys across the continent, found that around two-thirds of young Tunisians had considered emigrating.

The proportion who said they thought about leaving “a lot” rose from 38 percent in 2018 to 51 percent in 2024. Among young people considering emigration, 59 percent cited better job opportunities as their main motivation.

The findings point to frustration among a section of Tunisia’s youth and growing concerns about the prospects for professional and social stability at home.

The desire to leave extends beyond young people seeking their first jobs. Tunisia is also losing qualified professionals trained in the country.

Kamel Sahnoun, head of the Tunisian Order of Engineers, said at a press conference organised by the professional body that approximately 6,500 engineers left Tunisia in 2022 alone. The figure compares with an annual average of about 3,000 in 2013 and 2014, highlighting the scale of the departure of skilled workers.

The healthcare sector is also losing professionals.

Figures from the Tunisian Agency for Technical Cooperation show that 1,839 healthcare and paramedical professionals were recruited to work abroad in 2023. Another 1,022 were recruited during the first nine months of 2024, followed by 1,244 in 2025.

The figures, alongside international demand for Tunisian expertise, reflect the search for better working and living conditions abroad.

Hamza, a 26-year-old software engineer working for a foreign company, earns what he describes as a good income. Yet he is seriously considering leaving Tunisia.

“It’s no longer just about money,” he tells Al Jazeera.

His decision is shaped by several factors, including his lifestyle, his dealings with the administration, uncertainty about the future and the country’s broader economic situation.

Ramadan Ben Omar, a researcher specialising in migration, says the reasons people leave Tunisia have become more complex.

The motivations are no longer purely economic, he tells Al Jazeera. They also include the search for greater freedom, opportunities to participate in public life and the chance to build a better future.

Increasingly, he says, young people see emigration as a life project in its own right, rather than simply a way to improve their income.

Ben Omar also points to border areas such as Ben Guerdane, where accumulated economic and social pressures have prompted more young people to consider leaving through regular or irregular migration routes.

Maher has packed his bags for a new beginning in France. Hamza is weighing the decision despite his professional success. Ghaith is disappointed after years of waiting, while Mohamed Amine continues to believe in the possibility of reform.

Their contrasting experiences reflect a country grappling with economic difficulties and political uncertainty. For some, the prospect of a better life lies abroad; for others, hope for change at home remains.

The question facing Tunisia is whether it can offer its young people enough reason to stay.

articles.title: ‘You’ll see soon enough’: Trump on efforts to free US hostage held in Russia
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has hinted at a possible breakthrough in efforts to secure the release of an American hostage held in Russia.
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has hinted at a possible breakthrough in efforts to secure the release of an American hostage held in Russia. He also defended his decision to keep diplomatic negotiations with Russian president Vladimir Putin open on Ukraine, Iran, energy pipelines and hostages.Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday (local time), Trump said he was seeking the release of a hostage whose case had remained unresolved for years, suggesting that progress could emerge soon.“Well, you’ll see soon enough, because I’m trying to get a hostage that the country’s been after for a long time, and before my time,” Trump said when asked what assurances Putin had given that he wanted to reach a deal. “And let’s see what happens, that’ll be—that’ll be soon.”Trump’s remarks followed his statement on Sunday that negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict were making “great progress”. He defended his approach towards Moscow, arguing that imposing further penalties could undermine ongoing talks.“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations!”He added, “Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!”Earlier, Trump had signaled that he was willing to hold a high-stakes trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine and pursuing global denuclearisation, even if Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy was excluded from the negotiations. “Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody’s there or not", he said.Trump also cited Russia’s limited support for Iran amid escalating US economic and military pressure on Tehran as a reason to continue engaging with Moscow."Russia could have done a lot more to help, if you put it bluntly, Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia has done very little for Iran, and China could have done a lot more for Iran. They’ve done, and I remember that. When China does not that much, maybe nothing almost, but very little for Iran, and Russia does very little for Iran, I view that as being a very positive thing", he said.He added, “Russia’s done nothing there that we could see, and I think that’s a very positive.”Defending the broader negotiations, Trump said Washington was also discussing energy supplies and pipelines with Moscow, warning that he could withdraw from the process if the talks failed to deliver results.“And of course, we’re negotiating with him on Ukraine. So, I’m not looking to break up negotiations right in the middle,” he said. “And by the way, I have the right to do that at any time immediately. So if things don’t work out, I can always do it.”Trump’s outreach to Moscow has drawn criticism from some Republican lawmakers, particularly over sanctions and energy-related discussions. articles.title: Albanian PM warns of ‘red line’ after police station set ablaze
articles.summary: Albanian PM Edi Rama accused protesters of crossing a “red line” Monday after a police station was set ablaze during anti-govt demonstrations.
articles.body: Albanian PM Edi Rama accused protesters of crossing a “red line” Monday after a police station was set ablaze during anti-govt demonstrations.Demonstrators have clashed with police since last Tuesday as months of protests escalate, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and renewed calls for Rama’s resignation. “Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime; this red line must be drawn clearly at this critical stage of our democratic development,” Rama said.The PM said he was prepared for dialogue, except with those who commit violence and political parties that fail to distance themselves from it.Protesters again briefly clashed with police outside the education ministry Monday afternoon, after gathering in their hundreds from early morning. Demonstrators hurled stones at riot police, who responded with tear gas, forcing the crowd to disperse.“We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country,” Leka Sina, a 22-year-old science student, told AFP. “Violence is not a solution, but govt also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt,” he added.Across the demonstrations police have regularly used water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse crowds that have targeted govt buildings and smashed stores in several parts of the city. Around 300 people have been injured in the clashes, more than half of them police, according to the authorities.Source: AFPYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia puts off ‘Davos in the Desert’ summit to 2027 amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has postponed a major investment conference scheduled to take place in Riyadh next week, dealing a setback to the kingdom’s economic
articles.body: Saudi Arabia has postponed a major investment conference scheduled to take place in Riyadh next week, dealing a setback to the kingdom’s economic ambitions amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants.The future investment initiative (FII), widely known as “Davos in the Desert”, will now be held on an unspecified date in 2027, as reported by CNN.The annual gathering typically highlights Saudi Arabia’s financial strength and its expanding influence in global markets. Several prominent Wall Street executives, including JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon and BlackRock chief Larry Fink, were scheduled to address the event.However, organisers decided to call off the October 26-29 conference following a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital, including a deadly missile strike earlier this month targeting Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.Houthi attacks raise security concernsThe decision follows repeated Houthi missile and drone strikes targeting Saudi airports, energy facilities and other strategic locations. The attacks have also prompted several countries to issue travel advisories.Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants have exchanged missile, drone and air strikes on an almost daily basis in recent weeks, marking a sharp escalation in the conflict.The worsening security situation may also have raised concerns among corporate boards about sending their chief executives to Saudi Arabia while the country faces a deadly confrontation with the Houthis.In its statement, the FII Institute, which organises the conference, said the decision was made “to ensure that our milestone tenth edition delivers the full scale, quality and impact that our partners, members, speakers and delegates expect”.The organisers said the revised dates for the 2027 edition would be announced soon. They also confirmed that existing registrations and partnerships would remain valid.Setback for Saudi Arabia’s economic diversificationThe cancellation represents a setback for Saudi Arabia’s efforts to reduce its dependence on oil and natural gas by attracting international investment and expanding other sectors of its economy.The kingdom has spent decades seeking to draw western capital into the Middle East and strengthen its position as a global investment destination.However, the deteriorating security environment threatens to weaken those efforts and could usher in a period of investment uncertainty, with potential consequences extending beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘No fine, no admission of wrongdoing’: University of North Carolina strikes deal with Trump to end 18 probes
articles.summary: The administration of US President Donald Trump has reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC) to close 18 federal
articles.body: The administration of US President Donald Trump has reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC) to close 18 federal investigations into alleged race discrimination and antisemitism at the university. The voluntary agreement does not require any monetary payment, and UNC has not admitted to wrongdoing or liability.The deal, which remains in effect until the end of 2028, allows the university to retain its eligibility for federal funding. It comes amid the Trump administration’s broader crackdown on universities over pro-Palestinian protests against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, diversity initiatives, transgender policies and climate programmes.Unc to introduce mandatory antisemitism trainingUnder the agreement, UNC will appoint an internal administrator and establish a coordinator position within its compliance office to address discrimination, including antisemitism. The university has appointed Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, to fill both roles. She will also serve as the point of contact for the Justice Department and oversee the university’s reporting obligations.The settlement requires mandatory antisemitism training for students, faculty and staff. It also prohibits face masks or coverings that conceal an individual’s identity during protests and states that student groups may face disciplinary action for antisemitic discriminatory conduct.Trump has accused pro-Palestinian protesters of antisemitism and supporting extremism. However, protesters, including some Jewish groups, have argued that opposition to Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories and its military campaign in Gaza is not inherently antisemitic, and that advocating for Palestinian rights does not amount to supporting extremism.UNC will also be required to submit complaints involving antisemitism and race discrimination to the US Justice and Education departments every quarter.Unc must maintain non-discriminatory admissions policiesThe agreement requires UNC to maintain non-discriminatory admissions policies and prohibits the use of racial proxies. However, the university can consider how applicants have overcome personal adversity and take into account aspects of their family backgrounds, such as poverty, provided these factors are applied consistently.The settlement follows the US Supreme Court’s 2023 decision to strike down race-conscious admissions programmes at Harvard University and UNC, effectively ending the use of affirmative action in college admissions.Other universities have also reached settlements with the administration. Columbia University agreed last year to pay more than $200 million to resolve federal investigations, while Brown University agreed to pay $50 million to support local workforce development. articles.title: He was just 19 when Somali pirates captured his ship; Aman Kumar Sharma survived 43 months in captivity, a shipwreck and a desperate struggle to return home
articles.summary: When Aman Kumar Sharma left India in 2010 for his first voyage at sea, he was a 19-year-old from Himachal Pradesh beginning a career in the merchant navy.
articles.body: When Aman Kumar Sharma left India in 2010 for his first voyage at sea, he was a 19-year-old from Himachal Pradesh beginning a career in the merchant navy. He could not have imagined that his first assignment would turn into a 43-month ordeal involving armed pirates, brutal torture, the killing of a close friend, months spent in a Somali jungle and a shipwreck that nearly cost him his life.Sharma finally returned to India on June 9, 2014, after escaping captivity with 10 other crew members. Nearly four years after leaving home with hopes of building a career at sea, he returned to his family in Kangra, Himachal Pradesh, carrying memories that would take years to process.In a recent interview, Sharma revisited the hijacking of the MV Albedo, the desperate attempts to secure the crew’s release and the escape that brought his ordeal to an end. Today, he marks two birthdays: November 8, the day he was born, and June 9, the day he returned to India.“I try not to think of those days, and just thank God for the new life,” he told The Indian Express.His first voyage turned into a nightmareSharma joined the MV Albedo at Dubai’s Jebel Ali port in October 2010. The Iranian-owned, Malaysian-flagged vessel had a multinational crew, including two Indians. Its next port of call was Kenya, and the ship was sailing through waters known for piracy.The crew knew the route was risky, but leaving the ship was not a simple option. As Sharma recalled, “We had given the agent money for placement, so we couldn’t get off, though we knew it was a high-risk zone.”On November 26, 2010, at around 7.12 am, the crew spotted pirates approaching in a speedboat, roughly 200 nautical miles off the Maldives. They tried to secure the doors, but armed men boarded the vessel within minutes.The captain and third officer were captured, and the pirates threatened to kill the captain unless the remaining crew surrendered. The ship was subsequently forced towards Somalia, where the crew found themselves at the mercy of their captors.The pirates demanded a ransom of $20 million from the ship’s owner. As negotiations dragged on, the violence escalated. Crew members were beaten, officers were tortured and access to basic necessities was tightly controlled.“We need their permission even to use the washroom,” Sharma said, describing the restrictions imposed on the captives.The killing of his closest friendSeven months into captivity, ransom negotiations stalled. The pirates threatened to kill five crew members and gathered the men on the bridge. They then shot dead Raju Rajvar, the other Indian sailor on board and Sharma’s close friend, who had trained with him in Kolkata.The killing left the captives shocked and terrified. Sharma recalled that the pirates initially made them believe the incident might have been staged. The reality became clear when the crew were ordered to dispose of Rajvar’s body.“We were shocked – they were laughing. Initially we thought they faked the killing, but then when they called us to dispose of the body we froze.”The chief officer placed Rajvar’s body in a deep freezer, hoping that it might one day be returned to his family. The pirates then threatened Sharma himself. “They told me - you next,” he recalled.The experience left him emotionally numb. “What could I think after witnessing my friend being shot? I just reconciled to fate, so no emotions or fear; my mind was blank,” he said.Meanwhile, Sharma’s parents and sister tried to raise money through relatives, charities and non-governmental organisations. Efforts to negotiate a ransom continued, but proposed arrangements repeatedly fell apart.Six months in a Somali jungleAfter seven Pakistani crew members were released following a ransom payment, Sharma and the remaining captives were taken to a jungle near Harardhere in Somalia. They spent six months largely in the open, with limited water, little clothing and no certainty about when they would be freed.Their daily existence was marked by illness, deprivation and fear. “In the jungle, it was torture every day. We stayed in the open, slept under trees, and repeatedly fell sick. We had just two clothes - shorts and a T-shirt. We took a bath after 45 days, that too in hiding,” Sharma told the publication.In 2013, the captives were brought back to the ship amid hopes that a resolution might finally be possible. But the situation deteriorated again. The MV Albedo began taking on water as its cargo hold flooded. Four Bangladeshi crew members attempted to reach a distant trawler but drowned. Sharma, who could not swim, clung to a rope until a Cambodian fisherman rescued him.The ship sank, but survival did not mean freedom. The pirates took the remaining crew back to the jungle, where beatings resumed. Sharma was subjected to further torture, including having his nails pulled out.Another ransom attempt collapsed after a German captain tasked with delivering the money fled with it. Reflecting on the failed effort, Sharma asked: “If the UN could be cheated, what was the hope then?”The escape that brought him homeWith negotiations repeatedly failing, Sharma and the remaining crew members began planning their escape. They received help from a pirate who provided them with a phone and SIM card, allowing them to contact people in India and the United Nations.The crew decided to mix sleeping pills into their captors’ food. When the plan worked, the 11 remaining men cut an opening in their hut and fled at around 3 am, carrying documents salvaged from the sunken ship.A watchtower guard directed them towards a waiting vehicle. They continued walking until morning, when Somali government forces arrived and took them to a hotel, where they were given food and clothes.The following morning, a United Nations plane escorted by two American officials flew them to Kenya. Chirag Bahri of the International Seafarers’ Welfare and Assistance Network, who had helped coordinate efforts for their release, met them there.Sharma’s family travelled to receive him, and he finally returned to India on June 9, 2014.But coming home did not immediately end the ordeal. Sharma experienced nightmares, sensitivity to light and difficulty eating ordinary food. He realised he needed professional help and underwent counselling and psychiatric treatment.“I reached my home in Kangra, but recovery was slow. Nightmares, sensitivity to light, difficulty with ordinary food… I realised I required counselling and psychiatric help and underwent that too.” He said that understanding what his parents had endured during those years also gave him the willpower to recover.A second birthday, a new lifeSharma returned to work with Maersk in June 2015 and is now a bosun, a senior rating responsible for deck operations aboard a ship. He married in 2020 and has two children.The date of his return remains as significant as his birthday. November 8 marks the day he was born; June 9 marks the day he regained his freedom.For someone whose first voyage at sea became a prolonged fight for survival, the second date represents a life that continued despite years of uncertainty, violence and loss.His ordeal also comes amid renewed concerns about piracy off Somalia. As per recent reports, 2026 has seen a resurgence of hijackings involving Indian seafarers, underlining that the dangers Sharma faced more than a decade ago have not entirely disappeared.For Sharma, however, the most important milestone is personal: the day he came home and began rebuilding the life that captivity had interrupted.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes, exposing the
articles.body: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centres have disrupted banking, taxi services, food deliveries and digital access to homes, exposing the vulnerability of services used by millions of Russians. This comes as Kyiv expands its campaign against Moscow’s technology infrastructure.The attacks, carried out over several days in October, targeted data centres operated by Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, followed by a facility owned by Sberbank, the country’s largest bank. A data centre belonging to technology group VK was also reportedly targeted.Yandex, often described as “Russia’s Google”, provides search, email, navigation, music, ride-hailing, food delivery, cloud computing and digital payment services.Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30 per cent of normal levels following the October 8-11 strikes, The Moscow times reported, quoting internet monitoring group NetBlocks.Disruptions also affected third-party businesses that depend on its infrastructure, with users reporting problems accessing files, ordering taxis and entering residential buildings after digital keys stopped working.Yandex confirmed that one data centre had sustained significant damage, another had been shut down, and a third had suffered infrastructure disruptions.Although access to Yandex Pay was subsequently restored, several people reported that the service displayed an incorrect account balance.According to The Moscow Times, Yandex Pay remained only partially operational as of Monday, displaying a reassurance to users in place of the earlier error message: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”State agencies and private businesses relying on Yandex infrastructure, including dating apps and access systems for residential complexes and smart homes, also faced disruptions, The Moscow Times reported.Taxi drivers were also affected. Three drivers told NBC News they could not track their earnings or withdraw their money during the outage. One said the application had displayed error messages and, at times, dispatched multiple cars for a single customer.On October 14, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data centre in the Saratov region. However, the bank said its systems remained operational.“We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption,” Alexander Vedyakhin, Sberbank’s first deputy CEO told Reuters.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the government was discussing Yandex’s difficulties but that it was too early to assess whether users had suffered financial losses. Russia’s digital development minister Maksut Shadayev said officials were working with the defence ministry on measures to protect data centres, according to The Moscow Times.Ukraine has described the strikes as retaliation for Russian attacks on its own digital infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet”.The attacks have exposed the risks posed by Russia’s reliance on a relatively small number of major technology providers.Meanwhile, Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine’s digital and energy infrastructure. However, Russian data centres were potentially more vulnerable because many are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, whereas Ukraine’s are more widely dispersed. A strike on a single Russian facility can therefore disrupt services spanning payments, transport and internet access.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Rubio seeks to expand Central Asia ties with pomp-filled Uzbekistan visit
articles.summary: The Trump administration has portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — wedged between Russia, Iran and China — as a geopolitical battleground that deserves more attention.
articles.body: SAMARKAND, Uzbekistan — Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with counterparts from five Central Asian nations in Uzbekistan on Monday, a trip that resulted in relatively minor public deliverables, but which U.S. officials have presented as an opportunity to expand American soft power. Rubio, who arrived in the historic Silk Road city of Samarkand on Sunday night, met in the morning with the foreign ministers of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. In the evening, he dined with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and participated in a U.S.-Uzbekistan business council event. The Trump administration has portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — wedged between Russia, Iran and China — as a major geopolitical battleground that deserves more attention than it has received under previous administrations. U.S. officials have placed a particular emphasis on trying to secure greater access to the area’s rare earth mineral supplies, and Rubio came to Samarkand with more than 200 U.S. business leaders in tow, the State Department said. “I mean, look, it’s competition,” Rubio told journalists Monday morning after strolling through Registan Square, a complex of three imposing, azure-tiled madrassas that date to the Timurid Empire. “We have products, we have companies, they make things, and we just want fair competition and an opportunity.” Upon landing in Samarkand on Sunday night, Rubio was warmly embraced by Uzbekistan’s foreign minister, Bakhtiyor Saidov, while two women clad in elaborate gold-and-black traditional dresses presented him with a bouquet. In Registan Square on Monday, Rubio’s Uzbek hosts released hundreds of pigeons into the sky and filled the vast space with local pop music. Rubio’s trip comes at a fraught time in international affairs, and the secretary has faced questions from reporters about whether traveling to Uzbekistan is the best use of his time. Speaking to assembled business leaders on Monday night, Rubio appeared to address those criticisms, saying foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate crises, rather than ​build long-term relationships. “Our focus on a problem region or a problem country or a problem issue in the world still has to be there, but it cannot come at the expense of embracing opportunities,” Rubio said. “You have to be able to do both. Certainly, a large country and an influential country like the United States needs to be able to do both.” U.S.-Ukraine relations are at a low point after Washington urged Kyiv earlier in the month to stop striking Russian refineries and agreed to buy Russian diesel in a bid to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The war with Iran shows little sign of resolution, and U.S. ally Saudi Arabia has entered a disruptive war with Yemen’s Houthis. While European diplomats have often viewed Rubio as more supportive of Ukraine than Trump, in Samarkand he showed no signs of disagreeing with his boss, telling reporters that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should focus on ending the war and denying an assertion by Ukraine’s leader that the U.S. had paused intelligence sharing. There are indications that some of the Central Asian nations present, all of which are post-Soviet states, are deepening diplomatic and economic links with Washington. On Monday, Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords, a U.S.-led multilateral agreement that sets non-binding principles and legal guidelines for peaceful space exploration and resource management. The U.S. and Uzbekistan also signed an investment agreement across various sectors that the parties said would total $12 billion when implemented. But all five nations also maintain significant commercial and diplomatic links with Russia and, to varying extents, China and Iran, a fact that Rubio acknowledged. “Countries want to have as many relationships as possible,” Rubio told reporters while speaking alongside Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbekistan’s president and the head of the presidential office. “Uzbekistan’s been clear: They want to be friends to everybody.”
