articles.title: ‘US will burn like France’: Trump unleashes anti-immigrant tirade in bid to boost Republicans
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump invoked violent unrest in France to attack Democrats and rally support for Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, warning
articles.body: US President Donald Trump invoked violent unrest in France to attack Democrats and rally support for Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, warning that similar scenes could unfold in the United States if his political opponents prevail in the November 3 midterm elections.Earlier, Trump claimed he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron to close France’s borders, saying Paris would otherwise become a “Muslim city”.At a rally on Monday evening, Trump blamed immigration for the unrest in France, where protests over rising cost of living and declining purchasing power escalated into looting and clashes with police in several cities, according to Reuters.“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” Trump told the crowd.He described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists".“We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and ⁠raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”Speaking to reporters outside the White House earlier on Monday, Trump repeated his criticism of French president Emmanuel Macron’s immigration policies, claiming he had warned him years ago to tighten border controls.“Emanuel is a friend of mine. I told him a long time ago, ‘You’re making a big mistake in France. You’re letting everybody from the world come in. The whole world was coming in. Paris was going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal. That wasn’t the deal.’ I told him he should close up his borders. I’ve known him for eight or nine years, and I told him as soon as I met him,” Trump said.“Well, France, it is a very sad situation what’s happening in France, because what’s happening in France has to do with immigration, not schools, not anything. It’s immigration,” he said.Comparing France’s border policies with those of the United States, he said earlier, “I said you’re making a big mistake. We closed our borders; he didn’t. And you know what? His borders are a problem, and he also has a little bit of a problem with energy. But they are doing better than others. Emanuel should have closed his borders a long time ago. I told him to do it,” Trump told reporters.Nationwide demonstrations in France were called over the cost of living and pressure on household purchasing power. Reports of looting, fire and clashes prompted arrests and additional security measures, although the unrest’s causes extend beyond immigration.Trump’s remarks came as he campaigned for Marshall, who faces a competitive challenge from Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state that Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Economic discontent and opposition to Trump’s tariff policies have complicated the Republican incumbent’s re-election campaign, Reuters reported.Trump has also mocked Democrats by calling them “Dumocrats”. At the rally, Trump attacked Hamilton, saying, “He wants you to repent for being born White.” Marshall, meanwhile, criticised his opponent over cultural issues, calling him “too woke”.Economic concerns remain a challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms. A Reuters-Ipsos poll published on Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 31%, its lowest level in the survey.The November 3 elections will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress, with the Kansas contest emerging as one test of whether Trump’s immigration-focused messaging can offset voter concerns over prices and economic policy.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'No name in loan waiver list, daughter denied promised medical fee concession': Nanded farmer dies by suicide after video appeal to collector
articles.summary: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: A 46-year-old farmer from Borgaon Telang village in Maharashtra’s Nanded district allegedly died by suicide on Monday, shortly
articles.body: CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: A 46-year-old farmer from Borgaon Telang village in Maharashtra’s Nanded district allegedly died by suicide on Monday, shortly after recording and posting a video appealing to the district collector over his exclusion from government relief schemes.Shankar Abanrao Kshirsagar, who had cultivated soybean on his small landholding, said in the video that he had not benefited from successive farm loan-waiver announcements. He also claimed that his daughter, who is pursuing medical education in Pune, had not received the promised fee concession despite submitting an application.According to police, Kshirsagar’s relatives and the police began searching for him after the video came to their notice. He was subsequently found hanging in his field, where he had gone on Monday afternoon.“The farmer hanged himself in his field around 1pm on Monday, and his last rites were scheduled in the evening,” said Pandhari Bodhankar, in-charge of Borgaon police station. No offence had been registered in connection with the death till Monday night.Kshirsagar is survived by his wife, a son pursuing engineering studies and two daughters, one preparing for competitive examinations and the other studying medicine in Pune.Officials began verifying his financial circumstances and eligibility for government relief schemes after the incident. K B Fiske, deputy registrar of cooperative societies, said Kshirsagar had an outstanding crop loan of more than Rs 2 lakh with Maharashtra Gramin Bank.“His details reflect on the online database of govt and his name was expected to appear in the upcoming list of govt loan-waiver scheme,” Fiske said.Nanded collector Rahul Kardile ordered a detailed inquiry into the incident.The death has also raised concerns among farmer organisations over the implementation of drought-relief measures in Marathwada, where prolonged dry spells have damaged crops and added to the financial burden on cultivators.Ajit Nawale, national joint secretary of the Kisan Sabha, described the incident as a warning for the government and society.“The farmer suicide in Nanded is a warning sign for govt and society as a whole. The drought-relief measures must not remain on paper. Otherwise, more such unfortunate cases could happen,” he said.The incident comes amid a worsening drought situation in Marathwada. Of the region’s 76 talukas, 74 had earlier been declared drought-hit. Mukhed and Mudkhed in Nanded district, the remaining two talukas, were also recently brought under relief measures.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Speakerphone circus
articles.summary: Trains to planes, public transport these days can feel like a maniacal OTT experience.
articles.body: Trains to planes, public transport these days can feel like a maniacal OTT experience. Someone’s watching a C-drama and a belligerent TV anchor by turns, someone else raucous standup comedy, a person is abjectly face-timing their annoyed client in front of you, and another giving long-winded gyan on the magic of aloe vera , and he’s behind you. Those afflicted with ADD alongside exhibitionism, are scrolling through 25 reels a minute. There is a curious disappearance of embarrassment among these folk. No personal detail, medical or sexual, emotional or financial, is too personal not to be shared loudly. This is very much a minority of commuters, but they hold the rest of us hostage to their fancies.What explains their aversion to earphones and speaking softly? Maybe they think they’re doing some kind of social service because their taste is so ‘trendy’. Or they’re oblivious to the implicit social contract in public places. Or they’re too unimaginative to worry about what would happen if everyone behaved like them. For the sake of the rest of us, and the principle of mutual consideration, something does need to be done. Fines are a good idea. Whether it’s Singapore or Chennai, even implementation is what’s needed. UK is pursuing both fines and a “Share the journey, not the noise” campaign. Jail, however, as accented by Southern Railways, feels like a step too far. Every discord in ordinary public life shouldn’t be turned into a police matter.Weird thing is how long earphones were a settled part of public culture, before they became disputable. When the Walkman ruled the 1980s, or the iPod the 2000s, people walked down streets with their personal soundtrack, without imposing it on everyone else. We need to bring back that considerateness and impersonal civility. Civilisation, it now seems, is the slow process by which we relearn not to make strangers listen to our favourite songs.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Exclusive! Photographer Amrita Samant on capturing Suryakumar Yadav’s family moments; here's what the cricketer says
articles.summary: Explore Suryakumar Yadav's personal side as he embraces fatherhood in a heartwarming photoshoot with his wife and newborn daughter, captured by Amrita Samant.
articles.body: On the cricket field, Suryakumar Yadav is known for his audacious shots, quick footwork and fearless approach to the game. But away from the stadium lights and the roar of the crowd, the Indian cricketer is embracing a different role — that of a new father. Photographer Amrita Samant recently captured this quieter, more intimate side of SKY in a family photoshoot with his wife, Devisha, and their newborn daughter, who had just turned a month old when the shoot took place.For Amrita, who has spent years photographing children and families, the idea was not to capture the cricketer the world recognises, but the man his daughter will grow up knowing. “With .someone like Suryakumar, people are familiar with the cricketer, the extraordinary shots, the energy and the personality they see on the field. But my job is to look beyond that public persona and explore the person behind it, in this case, him being a new father to his gorgeous baby girl. What is he like when he’s not playing cricket? What does he look like when he’s relaxed, when he’s laughing, or when he’s interacting with his family? That’s a beautiful side to him that I get to see only in a shoot like this,” she says.Amrita recalls that Suryakumar and Devisha made the experience comfortable with their warmth and willingness to be themselves in front of the camera. For her, the success of such a shoot lies in making people forget that they are being photographed. “When you’re photographing someone like SKY, my intention isn’t to make him look like a cricketer or a celebrity. It’s to make him feel like himself. I want the photographs to tell this story about him that his child can view years later, not just the personality that everyone recognises online or on the field,” she explains.The photographer believes that the most meaningful frames often emerge when a conversation replaces instructions to pose. While working with the couple, she kept the conversation personal, focusing on their journey into parenthood. “For me, the real success of a shoot is when someone stops thinking about the camera. I do that by keeping a conversation going that’s personal, about the journey Devisha and him are on as parents, and that’s when I start seeing expressions and interactions that feel genuine. Those are the photographs that people connect with emotionally, because they feel like a memory,” she adds.Working with a newborn also meant that the shoot had to follow the baby's needs rather than a fixed schedule. Amrita says that children's natural personalities are best captured when they are allowed to be themselves, without being made to pose or smile on cue. Having photographed children for years, she approaches such sessions with patience, while ensuring that the newborn's comfort and safety remain the priority. “With SKY’s family shoot, it was with their beautiful newborn daughter who turned a month old when we shot together. Understanding the preparation before a newborn shoot, safety tips while handling a newborn and ensuring their baby is comfortable at all given times is of highest priority while planning their shoot. Their little one received the memo for their newborn shoot and performed to perfection,” she says with a laugh.For Suryakumar, too, the experience was less about posing for the camera and more about preserving a fleeting phase of family life. Unlike a brand campaign or a magazine cover, the family shoot offered him an opportunity to celebrate the simple joys he shares with Devisha and their daughter, away from the spotlight.“For me, a family photoshoot is so special — the simple joys of life I get to share with my wife and our daughter away from the spotlight. A newborn shoot gives us the chance to capture a little piece of our new life together! Unlike any professional photoshoot, this one was more about being ourselves and enjoying the chaos with our newborn baby,” he says.The cricketer admits that having everyone ready for the camera is not always as straightforward as it might seem. “Having my wife with our daughter makes the experience extra special, and some of the best pictures are often ones that happen naturally, without anyone trying too hard. As for posing, I’m quite comfortable in front of the camera, but getting Devisha camera-ready is always a challenge, and now with our daughter, we can plan all we want, but she has a schedule of her own! One has to be patient, go with the flow, and enjoy the little moments. These pictures are more than just photographs; they’re memories of a phase in our daughter’s life that we’ll want to look back on long after she’s grown up,” he says.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 10-year-old held a 6-year-old boy dangling from a chairlift about 16 feet above the ground for 4 minutes; he has now received the Carnegie Medal
articles.summary: A ski trip in Virginia took an unexpected turn on Jan.
articles.body: A ski trip in Virginia took an unexpected turn on Jan. 26, 2025, when a 6-year-old boy slipped off a moving chairlift and dangled above rough, sloping ground. Sitting beside him was Major Metzger, then 10, who grabbed the younger boy’s arms and held on until ski patrol reached them with a safety mat. The chair was about 16 feet above the ground, and the boy remained suspended for approximately 4 minutes. He eventually fell onto the mat, suffering a small bump on his head, and did not require further medical treatment. Metzger’s actions have since earned him the Carnegie Medal, one of North America’s highest honours for civilian heroism. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger presented the medal to him in September 2026, formally recognising a rescue that began with a child trying to keep his friend from falling.How Major Metzger held a 6-year-old boy above the groundAccording to the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission, the incident happened at a ski resort in Nellysford, Virginia, on Jan. 26, 2025. Six-year-old Bryce Rader was boarding a 4-person chairlift with 3 other children, including Metzger and their sisters. As the lift began moving uphill, Rader struggled to sit securely with his ski equipment. His helmet and skis added to the difficulty as he began sliding off the seat. Metzger, seated immediately beside him, grabbed him and tried to pull him back onto the chair. Workers were alerted and attempted to stop the lift, but Rader had already fallen completely off the seat by the time it came to a full stop. The bottom of the chair was about 16 feet above rugged, sloping ground.Metzger leaned forward and down, holding Rader’s arms with both gloved hands. He was wearing a helmet and skis himself, making the position particularly difficult as he tried to keep the younger boy from falling. He continued holding Rader while ski patrol made its way beneath the chair with a safety mat. Once rescuers were in position, they instructed Metzger to let go. Rader fell onto the mat and bounced off it, sustaining a small bump on his head. Medical staff evaluated him, but he did not need additional treatment and recovered. Metzger also made it safely off the lift. His arms were sore and he was shaken by the experience, although he did not require medical treatment. The Carnegie Hero Fund’s account documents the sequence of events, from Rader’s difficulty boarding to the moment ski patrol positioned the mat. It does not suggest that Metzger had time to plan his response. He acted as the situation unfolded and continued holding on until rescuers could reach the children.Carnegie Medal: what the civilian heroism award recognisesThe Carnegie Hero Fund Commission describes the Carnegie Medal as North America’s highest honour for civilian heroism. It recognises people in the United States and Canada who risk death or serious physical injury to an extraordinary degree while saving, or attempting to save, another person. The award is administered by the Pittsburgh-based Carnegie Hero Fund Commission, established by industrialist and philanthropist Andrew Carnegie in 1904. On March 24, 2026, the commission announced 18 new medal recipients, including Metzger. The announcement described the recognised acts as involving people who risked serious injury or death, or were killed, while trying to save others. The people saved by recipients in that round included 11 children.The Carnegie Hero Fund Commission’s latest award announcement puts the total number of Carnegie Medal recipients at 10,597 since the fund was established in 1904. The commission also reports that more than $47 million has been distributed through one-time grants, scholarship aid, death benefits and continuing assistance. The award is not limited to professional rescuers. Its purpose is to recognise extraordinary civilian acts in which people place themselves in danger to protect others. Metzger’s case illustrates how such an act can occur in an everyday setting, without specialist equipment or time to prepare.Other people recognised in the March 2026 announcement included Sean Hayes, a 33-year-old teacher who helped rescue a 15-year-old student set on fire at a school in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and Matt Vasey, a 54-year-old man who pulled the pilot from a floatplane that flipped over and crashed in a lake in Bellevue, Washington. The pilot later died from his injuries. The commission publishes individual citations describing the circumstances of each rescue, as well as information about its award consideration process.Major Metzger receives the Carnegie Medal in September 2026The medal announcement was not the final recognition of Metzger’s actions. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger presented Metzger with the Carnegie Medal in Virginia Beach on Sept. 16, 2026, according to a news release published by the governor’s office on Sept. 17. Spanberger praised Metzger’s courage, saying his actions represented the best of Virginia. The ceremony was attended by members of his family, school officials and local leaders.The presentation recognised an event that had occurred more than a year earlier, when Metzger was still 10. The official citation identifies Rader as the child he saved and records the date and location of the chairlift incident. The Carnegie Medal’s recognition of Metzger places his actions among a long history of civilian rescues involving fires, accidents, drowning incidents and other emergencies. In this case, the danger developed quickly, and the child who intervened was also exposed to the risk of falling.What the chairlift rescue showsThe incident highlights how quickly a routine ski outing can become an emergency, particularly when a young child struggles to sit securely on a moving lift. It also shows the importance of trained ski patrol teams and rescue equipment: patrol members brought a safety mat beneath the chair and directed the moment when Metzger should release his grip. The official account does not assign blame to the children or their families. Instead, it records how Metzger responded to his friend’s predicament and how rescuers helped bring the incident to a safe conclusion.For families, the practical lesson is to follow the individual resort’s chairlift instructions, ask lift staff for assistance when a child needs help boarding, and take concerns about a child’s ability to ride safely seriously. Specific procedures can vary by resort, so families should consult the resort’s own guidance rather than assume that one set of instructions applies everywhere. Metzger’s actions were recognised because he continued holding Rader until trained help was in position. His Carnegie Medal formally recognises the actions of a 10-year-old who held on to another child until ski patrol could assist.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
articles.summary: A group of parents claims local admission policy boosts Black and Latino students while constraining Asian applicants.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.

The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.

The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.

Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.

If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.

The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.

The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.

It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.

The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.

Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.

“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.

The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.

Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.

The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.

“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”

Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.
